..
Issued at 415 PM CDT Tue Sep 29 2026

Currently...

The first of several rounds of precipitation to impact the
forecast area made its way through the area last night into 
early this morning, dropping a swath of roughly 0.25-0.75in 
across the NWrn quarter of the forecast area. The next round is 
currently working its way northeast across the Central 
Plains...and will continue to do so through the rest of the day.
Upper air and satellite data showing these shortwave 
disturbances being ejected north east out ahead of the main 
western CONUS troughing and low pressure spinning over the 
CA/NV/AZ border area...while remnants of Hurricane Polo are 
working their way northeast into northern Mexico, providing an 
increased moisture source into the overall pattern. At the 
surface, it's an overall weak pattern across the forecast area, 
sitting between broad high pressure over the eastern CONUS and 
frontal boundary extending southwest from northern MN into the 
Desert SW. This is keeping winds generally southerly, and light 
around 5-10 MPH. 

Tonight through Thursday...

The main story for this 7-day forecast period remains squarely 
focused on this short term period through mid-week, with the
entire forecast area getting additional (but not necessarily 
welcomed) rainfall...with the potential for quite a gradient 
across the area. There hasn't been any significant changes in 
the general evolution of the next couple of days...with models 
remaining in good agreement showing the remnants of Polo 
becoming increasingly phased into the main upper trough axis/low
sitting over the Desert SW. Through this evening/tonight, while
the main upper low looks to only slide east into the AZ/NM 
border region by around 12Z Wed, that shortwave energy left over
from Polo is expected to continue on a northeastward trek out 
ahead of the main low...driving the next round of precipitation 
chances across our forecast area. 

Once the current batch of activity pushes further east...hi-res 
models showing a continued lull into tonight, especially across
the northern half of the forecast area. Increased low-mid 
level forcing (closer to 850-700mb) will keep better chances 
tonight focused across areas near the NE-KS state line...with 
some lingering, but important, uncertainties between models with
exactly where that axis sets up...important as that looks to be
the be first heavier band of rain to develop. Closer to, mainly
after 12Z Wednesday, models show that more widespread swath of 
precipitation to push north through the forecast area...with the
potential for a more distinct drop off on both the north and 
south sides than currently shown in the broader scale forecast. 
That could make the afternoon hours a bit more interesting on 
the southern side, with models showing a push of better 
instability also working its way north with time. Still some 
uncertainty with just how far north that lull in precip/better 
instability push and sfc frontal boundary gets, but it's not out
of the question that some additional convective 
enhancement/redevelopment occurs...and the southern half of the 
forecast area remains in the SPC Day 2 Marginal Risk area. Not 
looking at widespread severe weather...but gusty winds/hail 
possible, and with a sfc frontal boundary lingering in the area 
and more easterly winds, an isolated tornado is a concern as 
well. The overall main threat remains with heavy rain...and with
such a good fetch of moisture for this pattern to tap into, any
activity will be efficient rain-makers, even moreso for 
anything with any strength...and rates of 1-2 inches per hour is
certaintly not out of the question. 

Further into the evening/overnight hours Wednesday and Thursday,
the main push of the upper level system looks to pass through 
the Central Plains...again there is still some lingering overall
minor uncertainties with its exact track. Models aren't in too 
bad of agreement showing the upper low filling/weakening as it 
passes through during the day on Thursday...with precipitation 
chances dropping off fairly quickly during the second half of 
the day. Again some lingering uncertainties with exact 
timing...but current forecast as all but the far SSE dry by 
evening. 

By the time its all said and done...still looking at a fairly 
widespread area of 2-3 inches, with localized swaths of higher 
amounts (potentially much higher depending on the model). One of
the main changes in the models today is with increasing 
agreement focusing on the area with the better potential for 
those higher amounts (totals closer to 4-5 not out of the 
question)...running that axis mainly across the SSErn half of 
the forecast area. Some models have a more marked southward 
shift in the axis, clipping an even smaller portion of our SSErn
forecast area (showing more of an eastern KS and points NW 
issue). A result of both trends...a notably tighter rainfall 
gradient from north to south. Especially the further north one 
goes from I
